title: The Ring
full_review:
"The Ring" builds promisingly before burying itself in the well at which it winds up. Ehren Kruger based his screenplay on the first part of a Japanese trilogy that started with the 1998 "Ringu" and spawned a sequel and a prequel. All were adapted from stories by Koji Suzuki.

Naomi Watts, noted for her work in David Lynch's "Mulholland Drive," becomes caught in a mystery whose weirdness recalls such Lynch films but that strives for a more conventional approach, albeit a barely coherent one.

Watts portrays Rachel, who saves her job as a newspaper investigative reporter by promising a story about the bizarre suicides or murders of four teen-agers -- including her niece, Katie (Amber Tamblyn).

All of the teens died exactly seven days after watching a short, highly stylized video they'd been passing around. Each viewer was phoned immediately after the screening, promising death in precisely a week.

Rachel's young son, Aidan (David Dorfman), forecasted the death of cousin Katie by drawing pictures of a buried girl. With the aid of Aidan's father, the amiable Noah (Martin Henderson), Rachel begins her search for answers.

Why they broke up is as unclear as why her job was in
jeopardy at the beginning. Noah is a good father and a good companion. Individually, Rachel and Noah view the video and receive their death threats. She does most of the sleuthing, which is often difficult to follow because so much of the screenplay relies on coincidence, chance and illogical behavior.

Her search takes her to a ranch where the lonely, haunted Richard Morgan (Brian Cox) seems to withhold more information than he discloses.

Dr. Grasnick (Jane Alexander) is more forthcoming but apparently has less to offer.

With a lot of the dumb luck and poor judgment that has become indigenous to such low-aiming horror movies, Rachel wends her way to a solution that resolves some of her issues but that answers too few of the questions the audience has accumulated.

"The Ring" has some attractive Washington state photography, mostly in and around Seattle. Hans Zimmer's scoring adds a chilling touch, but director Gore Verbinski succumbs too frequently to the use of abrupt sound effects to spook the audience.

Viewers also may find tiresome the quantity of scenes that conclude just short of the disclosures toward which they've been building. It's a ploy that announces all too obviously that the movie is marking time rather than letting the audience participate in the unraveling of the mystery.

To broaden the audience base with a less restrictive PG-13 rating, the adult elements of sex, violence and language are not overdone.

Because of intermittent violence, an implied sexual encounter and some crude language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
(
2002
)
